source.text: קְֽרָא־נָ֭א הֲיֵ֣שׁ עוֹנֶ֑ךָּ וְאֶל־מִ֖י מִקְּדֹשִׁ֣ים תִּפְנֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Call please; [is] there [one] answering you? And to which of [the] holy [ones] will you turn?

en.L: Call, please; is there [anyone] answering you? \q And to which of [the] holy ones will you turn?
en.B: Call out, then; is there anyone who will answer you? \q To which of the holy ones will you turn?
en.R: Go ahead and call for help, but will anyone answer you? \q Which of the heavenly beings will you turn to?

decisions.choice: the holy ones: heavenly beings, God's attendants
decisions.reason: "Holy ones" is a name for the beings who stand around God in heaven (Job 15:15; Psalm 89:6, 8; Zechariah 14:5). Eliphaz has just said that God finds fault even with his servants and messengers (4:18), so no heavenly being will take Job's side against God.

decisions.choice: a challenge: call, but no one will answer
alternatives: a sincere suggestion to pray to the holy ones
decisions.reason: The word "please" (na') softens the command, but the question that follows expects the answer "no one". Eliphaz is not telling Job to appeal to angels; he is saying that no appeal against God will be heard.

decisions.choice: the heavenly beings
decisions.reason: Readable says "heavenly beings", the same words it uses for "the sons of God" in Job 1:6, because "holy ones" alone could be taken for holy people on earth (m1).

source.text: כִּֽי־לֶֽ֭אֱוִיל יַהֲרָג־כָּ֑עַשׂ וּ֝פֹתֶ֗ה תָּמִ֥ית קִנְאָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: For [to] a fool kills vexation, and a simple [one] slays jealousy.

en.L: For vexation kills the fool, \q and jealousy slays the simple.
en.B: For resentment kills the fool, \q and envy slays the simple.
en.R: Anger kills a foolish person, \q and jealousy kills someone who is easily led.

decisions.choice: the fool is the one who is killed
decisions.reason: The little word "to" (le) here marks the object of the verb, as it often does in later Hebrew and in Aramaic: vexation kills the fool. The second line has the same shape: jealousy kills the simple.

decisions.choice: vexation: brooding, angry grief; jealousy: hot, passionate feeling
decisions.reason: Ka'as is the anger and grief that a person nurses inside (1 Samuel 1:6, 16; Proverbs 27:3). Qin'ah is any burning passion: jealousy, envy, or zeal. Eliphaz is warning Job: his angry complaint (chapter 3) is the kind of thing that destroys fools. Job takes up the same word ka'as in 6:2.

decisions.choice: the simple: a naive person, easily led
decisions.reason: The simple person (poteh) is the inexperienced one who believes anything and is easily misled, as often in Proverbs (Proverbs 1:4, 22; 14:15).

decisions.choice: resentment
decisions.reason: "Vexation" is rare in modern speech. "Resentment" names the brooding anger that the word means (m2).

source.text: אֲֽנִי־רָ֭אִיתִי אֱוִ֣יל מַשְׁרִ֑ישׁ וָאֶקּ֖וֹב נָוֵ֣הוּ פִתְאֹֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: I, I have seen [a] fool taking root, and I cursed his dwelling suddenly.

en.L: I have seen a fool taking root, \q and suddenly I cursed his dwelling.
en.B: I myself have seen a fool putting down roots, \q but suddenly I declared his home cursed.
en.R: I have seen a foolish man doing well, like a plant putting down roots, \q but right away I said his home was cursed.

decisions.choice: taking root: settling in and doing well
decisions.reason: A plant that takes root is established and thriving; the picture is used for people who prosper (Psalm 37:35; Jeremiah 12:2). For a time the fool seemed secure.

decisions.choice: I cursed: I declared his home doomed, at once
alternatives: his home was suddenly cursed (a slightly different text)
I cursed it in my heart
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "I cursed": Eliphaz, seeing the fool prosper, pronounced his home doomed, and the next verses describe what then happened to it. Some ancient translations read "his home was suddenly cursed" (or "rotted"), which needs a small change to the text. "Suddenly" may belong to the curse (at once) or to the ruin that came on the home.

decisions.choice: dwelling: home, homestead
decisions.reason: Naveh can be a pasture or a dwelling place; here, as in 5:24 and 18:15, it is a person's home and all that goes with it.

decisions.choice: doing well, like a plant putting down roots
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture (m1) so that a young reader does not take it literally.

source.text: יִרְחֲק֣וּ בָנָ֣יו מִיֶּ֑שַׁע וְיִֽדַּכְּא֥וּ בַ֝שַּׁ֗עַר וְאֵ֣ין מַצִּֽיל׃

records.literal_gloss: Far are his sons from safety, and they are crushed in [the] gate, and there is no deliverer.

en.L: His sons are far from safety, \q and they are crushed in the gate, \q and there is no one delivering [them].
en.B: His children are far from safety; \q they are crushed in the court at the gate, \q with no one to rescue them.
en.R: His children are never safe. \q They are crushed in court, and no one is there to rescue them.

decisions.choice: the gate: the place where cases were judged
alternatives: the city gate as a place of battle
decisions.reason: The elders of a town sat in the gate to hear disputes and give judgment (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1-11; Amos 5:12, 15). To be crushed in the gate is to lose one's case and be wronged by the court, with no one to speak up for you.

decisions.choice: his sons: his children, his family after him
decisions.reason: The word (banim) is "sons", but the point is the fool's whole family line: his household does not escape the ruin.

decisions.choice: safety: help, deliverance
decisions.reason: Yesha' is rescue and the safety it brings; the same word ends 5:11.

decisions.choice: the court at the gate
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "court" so that the reader sees why being crushed in the gate matters (m1).

source.text: אֲשֶׁ֤ר קְצִיר֨וֹ׀רָ֘עֵ֤ב יֹאכֵ֗ל וְאֶֽל־מִצִּנִּ֥ים יִקָּחֵ֑הוּ וְשָׁאַ֖ף צַמִּ֣ים חֵילָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Whose harvest [the] hungry eats, and even from thorns he takes it, and a snare pants [for] their wealth.

en.L: Whose harvest [the] hungry eats, \q and even from among thorns he takes it, \q and a snare gapes for their wealth.
en.B: The hungry eat up his harvest, \q taking it even from among the thorns, \q and a trap lies open for their wealth.
en.R: Hungry people eat his harvest; \q they take it even from among the thorns. \q Their wealth is snapped up as if in a trap.

decisions.choice: a snare: a trap waiting for their wealth
alternatives: the thirsty pant for their wealth
decisions.reason: The vowels of the Hebrew text give tsammim, a snare or trap (Job 18:9). With other vowels the same letters read "the thirsty", which makes a pair with "the hungry" in the first line, and several ancient translations read it so. Either way the fool's family loses what it owns.

decisions.choice: even from among thorns: nothing stops the hungry
decisions.reason: The words "and to, from thorns" are hard. The most likely sense is that the hungry take the crop even where it grows among thorns, or behind the thorn hedge that protected a field. The point is clear: nothing he has is safe.

decisions.choice: their wealth: the fool's household's
decisions.reason: The verse moves from "his" harvest to "their" wealth: the fool and his children (5:4) lose everything together.

decisions.choice: Their wealth is snapped up as if in a trap
alternatives: a snare gapes for their wealth
decisions.reason: Readable puts the wealth first and makes the trap a comparison, which is easier to follow than a trap that gapes.

source.text: כִּ֤י׀לֹא־יֵצֵ֣א מֵעָפָ֣ר אָ֑וֶן וּ֝מֵאֲדָמָ֗ה לֹא־יִצְמַ֥ח עָמָֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: For not goes out from the dust trouble, and from the ground not sprouts toil.

en.L: For trouble does not come out of the dust, \q and toil does not sprout from the ground.
en.B: Hardship does not spring up from the dust, \q and trouble does not sprout from the soil.
en.R: Trouble does not grow up out of the dust, \q and hardship does not sprout from the ground.

decisions.choice: trouble and toil: harm, with a hint of wrongdoing
decisions.reason: 'Aven can mean trouble or the wickedness that causes it; 'amal is hard toil and the misery it brings. Eliphaz has already said that those who plow 'aven reap 'amal (4:8). Trouble is not a weed that comes up by itself.

decisions.choice: for: this explains verses 2-5
decisions.reason: The verse gives the reason behind the fool's ruin: trouble has a cause. Verse 7 then says where it comes from.

decisions.choice: no "for" at the start
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable leave the linking word unexpressed; the order of the lines already shows the connection. Literal keeps it.

source.text: כִּֽי־אָ֭דָם לְעָמָ֣ל יוּלָּ֑ד וּבְנֵי־רֶ֝֗שֶׁף יַגְבִּ֥יהוּ עֽוּף׃

records.literal_gloss: For man to trouble is born, and [the] sons of flame make high to fly.

en.L: But {{gender:a human|man}} is born to trouble, \q and sons of flame fly high.
en.B: No, {{gender:human beings are|man is}} born to trouble, \q as sparks fly upward.
en.R: {{gender:People are|Man is}} born to have trouble, \q just as sparks always fly up from a fire.

decisions.choice: but rather: after a negative, it gives the true cause
decisions.reason: After "trouble does not come out of the dust" (verse 6), ki means "no, but": trouble comes from human beings themselves, not from the ground.

decisions.choice: is born to trouble
decisions.reason: The vowels of the Hebrew text read "is born". With other vowels the same letters read "begets": human beings breed their own trouble, which would follow verse 6 even more closely. The written vowels are kept; both say that trouble is part of human life.

decisions.choice: sons of flame: sparks
decisions.reason: "Sons of" names what belongs to a thing, so the sons of a flame (reshef) are sparks. Reshef can also mean a burning bolt or pestilence (Deuteronomy 32:24; Habakkuk 3:5), and some take the line as birds of prey soaring. Sparks fit best: they rise from a fire as surely as trouble comes to people.

decisions.choice: man: any human being
decisions.reason: 'Adam is humankind, every person, not a male only.

decisions.choice: as sparks fly upward
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets the two lines side by side with "and"; Balanced and Readable make the comparison plain with "as".

source.text: אוּלָ֗ם אֲ֭נִי אֶדְרֹ֣שׁ אֶל־אֵ֑ל וְאֶל־אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים אָשִׂ֥ים דִּבְרָתִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: But I, I would seek to God, and to God I would set my cause,

en.L: But as for me, I would seek God, \q and to God I would commit my cause,
en.B: But as for me, I would turn to God \q and lay my case before God.
en.R: If I were you, I would turn to God \q and bring my case to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: I would: advice, what Eliphaz would do in Job's place
alternatives: I will seek God (a statement of Eliphaz's own plan)
decisions.reason: The verb form can mean "I will" or "I would". The emphatic "but I" sets Eliphaz against the fool and against Job's complaint: if he were in Job's place, he would bring his case to God.

decisions.choice: God, God: two words for the one God
decisions.reason: The first line has 'El and the second 'Elohim; Hebrew poetry often varies the word in parallel lines. Both mean God.

decisions.choice: my cause: my case, my complaint
decisions.reason: Dibrah is a matter or cause, here a case laid before a judge. Eliphaz uses the language of the law court, which Job will take up (9:3; 13:3, 18).

decisions.choice: If I were you
decisions.reason: Readable makes the advice plain (m1).

decisions.choice: the verse ends with a full stop
alternatives: a comma, running on into verse 9
decisions.reason: Verse 9 describes God with a participle, "who does great things", so in Hebrew the sentence runs on. Literal keeps the comma; Balanced and Readable start a new sentence with "He" in verse 9.

source.text: עֹשֶׂ֣ה גְ֭דֹלוֹת וְאֵ֣ין חֵ֑קֶר נִ֝פְלָא֗וֹת עַד־אֵ֥ין מִסְפָּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: [who] does great [things] and [there is] no searching, wonders until [there is] no number.

en.L: who does great things, and [there is] no searching [them out], \q wonders until [there is] no number.
en.B: He does great things beyond understanding, \q wonders that cannot be counted.
en.R: He does great things that no one can understand, \q more wonderful things than anyone can count.

decisions.choice: who does: the first of a row of descriptions of God
decisions.reason: Verses 9-16 are a short hymn: a string of participles ("who does", "who gives", "who frustrates") describing God. Job repeats this line almost word for word in 9:10, but to say that God's power is frightening.

decisions.choice: no searching: beyond finding out
decisions.reason: "There is no searching" means that no one can search them out or fathom them (Psalm 145:3; Isaiah 40:28).

decisions.choice: He does
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable begin a new sentence and supply "He" for the participle (see 5:8).

source.text: הַנֹּתֵ֣ן מָ֭טָר עַל־פְּנֵי־אָ֑רֶץ וְשֹׁ֥לֵֽחַ מַ֝יִם עַל־פְּנֵ֥י חוּצֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: the [one who] gives rain on [the] face of [the] earth, and sends water on [the] face of [the] open places,

en.L: who gives rain on [the] face of [the] earth \q and sends water on [the] face of [the] fields,
en.B: He gives rain to the earth \q and sends water on the fields.
en.R: He sends rain on the earth \q and waters the fields.

decisions.choice: the open places: the fields and open country
decisions.reason: Chutsot is what lies outside: in a town the streets, in the country the fields beyond the town. Here it stands beside "the earth", so it means the open land.

decisions.choice: rain as God's gift
decisions.reason: Rain is the gift by which God keeps the land alive (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24). When God answers Job, he asks who gives the rain (38:25-28).

decisions.choice: to the earth, on the fields
alternatives: on the face of the earth
decisions.reason: "The face of" is the Hebrew way of saying "the surface of"; Balanced and Readable leave it out. Literal keeps it.

source.text: לָשׂ֣וּם שְׁפָלִ֣ים לְמָר֑וֹם וְ֝קֹדְרִ֗ים שָׂ֣גְבוּ יֶֽשַׁע׃

records.literal_gloss: to set [the] lowly on high, and mourners are high [in] safety.

en.L: to set [the] lowly on high, \q and [those] mourning are lifted to safety.
en.B: He sets the lowly on high, \q and those who mourn are lifted to safety.
en.R: He raises up people who are humble, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lifts those who are sad to a safe place.

decisions.choice: to set: another thing God does, or the purpose of the rain
decisions.reason: The verb is an infinitive, "to set". It continues the list of God's acts; some take it as the purpose of the rain in verse 10 (he sends rain so as to raise the lowly). The meaning is much the same.

decisions.choice: mourners: those dressed in dark clothes of grief
decisions.reason: Qoderim are literally "the dark ones": people in mourning, unwashed and in dark clothing (Psalm 35:14; 38:7). The same word describes dark streams in 6:16.

decisions.choice: God lifts the lowly
decisions.reason: The same hope is sung in 1 Samuel 2:7-8 and Psalm 113:7-8: God brings down the proud and raises the poor.

decisions.choice: He sets
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the infinitive a plain sentence (m1).

source.text: מֵ֭פֵר מַחְשְׁב֣וֹת עֲרוּמִ֑ים וְֽלֹא־תַעֲשֶׂ֥ינָה יְ֝דֵיהֶ֗ם תּוּשִׁיָּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [who] frustrates [the] plans of [the] crafty, and their hands do not achieve success.

en.L: [He] frustrates [the] plans of [the] crafty, \q and their hands do not achieve success.
en.B: He thwarts the schemes of the crafty, \q so that their hands achieve nothing.
en.R: He spoils the plans of tricky people, \q so they cannot carry them out.

decisions.choice: crafty: cunning, scheming
decisions.reason: 'Arum can be good (prudent, Proverbs 12:16, 23) or bad (cunning, as the serpent in Genesis 3:1). Here it is the bad sense: people whose clever plans work against others.

decisions.choice: success: effective wisdom, a plan that works
decisions.reason: Tushiyyah is a wisdom word for what really works, practical success (Job 6:13; Proverbs 2:7; 3:21). The schemer's hands never get that far.

decisions.choice: achieve nothing
decisions.reason: Balanced says the result plainly; Literal keeps "success".

source.text: לֹכֵ֣ד חֲכָמִ֣ים בְּעָרְמָ֑ם וַעֲצַ֖ת נִפְתָּלִ֣ים נִמְהָֽרָה׃

records.literal_gloss: [who] catches [the] wise in their craftiness, and [the] counsel of [the] twisted [ones] is hurried.

en.L: [He] catches [the] wise in their craftiness, \q and [the] counsel of [the] twisted is rushed [to its end].
en.B: He catches the wise in their own cunning, \q and the schemes of the devious are swept away.
en.R: He traps clever people with their own tricks, \q and the plans of dishonest people quickly fall apart.

decisions.choice: quoted by Paul
decisions.reason: Paul quotes the first line in 1 Corinthians 3:19, "He catches the wise in their craftiness". It is the one clear quotation of Job in the New Testament. Paul accepts the truth of Eliphaz's words even though, at the end, God says the friends did not speak rightly of him (42:7).

decisions.choice: the twisted: devious, crooked people
decisions.reason: Niftalim are those who twist and wrestle (the same root as Genesis 30:8; Proverbs 8:8): crooked in their dealings.

decisions.choice: hurried: their plan is carried along too fast and comes to nothing
decisions.reason: Nimharah means rushed, hasty. The schemers' plan is swept headlong, before it can succeed, and so it fails.

decisions.choice: are swept away
decisions.reason: Balanced says what the hurry leads to (m3); Literal keeps "rushed".

source.text: יוֹמָ֥ם יְפַגְּשׁוּ־חֹ֑שֶׁךְ וְ֝כַלַּ֗יְלָה יְֽמַשְׁשׁ֥וּ בַֽצָּהֳרָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: By day they meet darkness, and as [at] night they grope at noon.

en.L: By day they meet darkness, \q and as [at] night they grope at noon.
en.B: In the daytime they run into darkness, \q and at noon they grope as if it were night.
en.R: Even in the daytime it is dark for them; \q at noon they feel their way around as if it were night.

decisions.choice: groping at noon: a covenant curse
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 28:29 warns that the disobedient will grope at noon as the blind grope in the dark. The crafty, for all their cleverness, cannot see their way.

decisions.choice: darkness by day: confusion, being lost
decisions.reason: Darkness at the time of light is a picture of complete confusion and failure (Isaiah 59:10).

source.text: וַיֹּ֣שַׁע מֵ֭חֶרֶב מִפִּיהֶ֑ם וּמִיַּ֖ד חָזָ֣ק אֶבְיֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And he saves from [the] sword, from their mouth, and from [the] hand of [the] strong [the] needy.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} saves from [the] sword, from their mouth, \q and from [the] hand of [the] strong, [the] needy.
en.B: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} saves the needy from the sword of their mouths \q and from the grip of the powerful.
en.R: But God saves people in need from the cutting words of the powerful \q and from their grip.

decisions.choice: from the sword, from their mouth: the sword that is their mouth
alternatives: from the sword of their mouth, and the orphan from the hand of the strong (a slightly different text)
decisions.reason: The two phrases stand side by side: the sword is the mouth of the crafty, their harsh and lying words (Psalm 57:5; 59:8; 64:4). Some read one letter differently and get "the orphan" in place of "from their mouth", to pair with "the needy". The text as it stands makes good sense.

decisions.choice: the needy: the poor, those who depend on others
decisions.reason: 'Evyon is the poor person who has no means of his own (Deuteronomy 15:4, 11). The word stands at the end and belongs to both lines: God rescues the needy from the sword and from the strong hand.

decisions.choice: the hand of the strong: their power
decisions.reason: "Hand" often stands for power or control (5:20; 6:23).

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Readable names God, since the subject is several verses back (5:8).

source.text: וַתְּהִ֣י לַדַּ֣ל תִּקְוָ֑ה וְ֝עֹלָ֗תָה קָ֣פְצָה פִּֽיהָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And there is for the poor hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.

en.L: So there is hope for the poor, \q and injustice shuts its mouth.
en.B: So the poor have hope, \q and injustice shuts its mouth.
en.R: So poor people have hope, \q and wrongdoing is silenced.

decisions.choice: injustice shuts its mouth
decisions.reason: Psalm 107:42 uses the same picture: when God lifts the needy, all wickedness shuts its mouth. Injustice is pictured as a person who had much to say and now falls silent.

decisions.choice: the poor: the weak, those of low standing
decisions.reason: Dal is someone poor and powerless, without influence (Leviticus 14:21; Proverbs 22:22).

decisions.choice: so: the result of God's rescue
decisions.reason: The verb continues the story of verse 15: because God saves the needy, the poor have hope.

decisions.choice: wrongdoing is silenced
decisions.reason: Readable says what the picture means (m1).

source.text: הִנֵּ֤ה אַשְׁרֵ֣י אֱ֭נוֹשׁ יוֹכִחֶ֣נּֽוּ אֱל֑וֹהַּ וּמוּסַ֥ר שַׁ֝דַּ֗י אַל־תִּמְאָֽס׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, how blessed [is] [the] person [whom] God reproves; and [the] discipline of [the] Almighty do not reject.

en.L: Look, how blessed [is] {{gender:the person|the man}} whom God corrects; \q so do not reject [the] discipline of the Almighty.
en.B: How blessed is {{gender:the one|the man}} whom God corrects! \q So do not reject the discipline of the Almighty.
en.R: The person God corrects is truly blessed, \q so do not refuse it when God All-Powerful disciplines you.

decisions.choice: how blessed: an exclamation about a life that goes well
decisions.reason: The word ('ashre) is the one that opens Psalm 1: "oh, the blessings of ...". Eliphaz says that God's correction is a sign of his care, not of his rejection.

decisions.choice: the Almighty: Shaddai, an ancient name of God
decisions.reason: Shaddai is one of the oldest names of God, used by the patriarchs (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3), and it appears more often in Job than in any other book. Its origin is uncertain; since the ancient Greek translation it has been taken as "the Almighty". This is its first use in Job.

decisions.choice: the discipline of the Lord
decisions.reason: Proverbs 3:11-12 says the same thing in nearly the same words: do not reject the Lord's discipline, for he corrects the one he loves; Hebrews 12:5-6 quotes Proverbs. Eliphaz assumes that Job is being corrected for some fault; the reader knows from chapters 1-2 that this is not why Job suffers.

decisions.choice: the person: any human being
decisions.reason: 'Enosh is a human being, frail and mortal, not only a male.

decisions.choice: God All-Powerful
decisions.reason: Readable says "God All-Powerful" for Shaddai in every book, so that a young reader knows the name refers to God.

decisions.choice: no "Look"
decisions.reason: Hinneh draws attention; Balanced and Readable carry it with the exclamation instead of a separate word. Literal keeps "Look".

source.text: כִּ֤י ה֣וּא יַכְאִ֣יב וְיֶחְבָּ֑שׁ יִ֝מְחַ֗ץ וְיָדָ֥יו תִּרְפֶּֽינָה׃

records.literal_gloss: For he causes pain and he binds up; he smashes, and his hands heal.

en.L: For {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} causes pain and binds up; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} strikes, and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands heal.
en.B: For {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wounds, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} also binds up; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} strikes, but {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands heal.
en.R: God may hurt you, but then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} bandages the wound; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} strikes, but {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands bring healing.

decisions.choice: God wounds and heals
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 32:39 ("I wound and I heal") and Hosea 6:1 ("he has torn us, and he will heal us") say the same: the God who strikes is the God who restores.

decisions.choice: his hands, as the scribes' reading has it
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) read "his hand"; the reading the scribes marked (qere) is "his hands". The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: he: God himself, with emphasis
decisions.reason: The pronoun is written out for emphasis: the one who wounds is the very one who heals.

decisions.choice: God may hurt you
decisions.reason: Readable names God and the person hurt, which the Hebrew leaves to the context.

source.text: בְּשֵׁ֣שׁ צָ֭רוֹת יַצִּילֶ֑ךָּ וּבְשֶׁ֓בַע׀לֹא־יִגַּ֖ע בְּךָ֣ רָֽע׃

records.literal_gloss: In six troubles he will deliver you, and in seven not will touch you harm.

en.L: In six troubles {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will deliver you, \q and in seven, harm will not touch you.
en.B: He will rescue you from six troubles; \q in seven, no harm will touch you.
en.R: He will rescue you from trouble again and again; \q no matter how many times, nothing bad will touch you.

decisions.choice: six, seven: trouble after trouble, as many as there are
decisions.reason: A number followed by the next number is a way of saying "many" or "every one" in Hebrew poetry (Proverbs 6:16; 30:15-31; Amos 1:3). The point is not the count but that God's help never runs out.

decisions.choice: harm: evil, anything bad
decisions.reason: Ra' covers both moral evil and misfortune; here it is harm that happens to a person.

decisions.choice: again and again, no matter how many times
decisions.reason: Readable explains the number saying (m1).

source.text: בְּ֭רָעָב פָּֽדְךָ֣ מִמָּ֑וֶת וּ֝בְמִלְחָמָ֗ה מִ֣ידֵי חָֽרֶב׃

records.literal_gloss: In famine he will ransom you from death, and in battle from [the] hands of [the] sword.

en.L: In famine {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will ransom you from death, \q and in war from [the] hands of [the] sword.
en.B: In famine {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will redeem you from death, \q and in war from the power of the sword.
en.R: When there is no food, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will save you from dying; \q in war {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will keep you from being killed.

decisions.choice: ransom: set free, rescue
decisions.reason: Padah is to free someone, often by a payment, but when God is the subject no price is named (Deuteronomy 7:8; Psalm 25:22). Job will use the word in 6:23.

decisions.choice: a past form for a sure future
decisions.reason: The verb is in the form normally used for completed action; here it states as certain what God will do.

decisions.choice: the hands of the sword: the power of the sword
decisions.reason: The sword is pictured with hands; it means death in battle. The reader remembers that Job's servants were killed by the sword (1:15, 17).

decisions.choice: keep you from being killed
alternatives: from the hands of the sword
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the picture means (m3).

source.text: בְּשׁ֣וֹט לָ֭שׁוֹן תֵּחָבֵ֑א וְֽלֹא־תִירָ֥א מִ֝שֹּׁ֗ד כִּ֣י יָבֽוֹא׃

records.literal_gloss: In [the] whip of [the] tongue you will be hidden, and not you will be afraid of destruction when it comes.

en.L: From [the] whip of [the] tongue you will be hidden, \q and you will not be afraid of destruction when it comes.
en.B: You will be sheltered from the lash of the tongue, \q and you will not fear destruction when it comes.
en.R: You will be protected when people attack you with words, \q and you will not be afraid when disaster comes.

decisions.choice: the whip of the tongue: slander, wounding words
decisions.reason: Words that wound are pictured as a whip (Psalm 31:21; Jeremiah 18:18). God will hide the righteous from them.

decisions.choice: destruction: violent ruin, devastation
decisions.reason: Shod is ruin that falls suddenly, by raiders or by storm (Isaiah 13:6). The same word begins verse 22.

decisions.choice: when people attack you with words
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture (m1).

source.text: לְשֹׁ֣ד וּלְכָפָ֣ן תִּשְׂחָ֑ק וּֽמֵחַיַּ֥ת הָ֝אָ֗רֶץ אַל־תִּירָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: At destruction and at famine you will laugh, and of [the] beasts of the earth do not be afraid.

en.L: At destruction and at famine you will laugh, \q and of [the] beasts of the earth you need not be afraid.
en.B: You will laugh at destruction and hunger, \q and you need not fear the wild animals of the earth.
en.R: You will laugh at disaster and hunger, \q and you will not be afraid of wild animals.

decisions.choice: laugh: be unafraid, confident
decisions.reason: To laugh at a danger is to have no fear of it (Job 39:7, 18, 22; 41:21).

decisions.choice: famine: hunger
decisions.reason: Kafan is a rare word for famine, different from the word in verse 20; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: do not be afraid: an assurance, you need not fear
decisions.reason: The negative with this verb form is usually a command, but in a list of promises it reassures: there will be nothing to fear.

decisions.choice: you need not be afraid
decisions.reason: "Need not" keeps the sense of reassurance (m3) and the flow of the promises.

source.text: כִּ֤י עִם־אַבְנֵ֣י הַשָּׂדֶ֣ה בְרִיתֶ֑ךָ וְחַיַּ֥ת הַ֝שָּׂדֶ֗ה הָשְׁלְמָה־לָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: For with [the] stones of the field [will be] your covenant, and [the] beasts of the field will be at peace with you.

en.L: For with the stones of the field [will be] your covenant, \q and the beasts of the field will be at peace with you.
en.B: For you will be in covenant with the stones of the field, \q and the wild animals will be at peace with you.
en.R: You will be at peace even with the stones in your fields, \q and the wild animals will live at peace with you.

decisions.choice: a covenant with the stones: the land itself will not work against you
alternatives: the stones will be your allies
decisions.reason: Stones in a field spoil the ground for plowing (2 Kings 3:19, 25; Isaiah 5:2). To be in covenant with them means they will do no harm to your crops: creation itself will be at peace with the righteous, as in Hosea 2:20 and Isaiah 11:6-9.

decisions.choice: the beasts of the field: wild animals
decisions.reason: "Animals of the field" are the wild animals, as in verse 22.

decisions.choice: be at peace: be brought into peace with you
decisions.reason: The verb (from shalem) is passive: the animals are made to be at peace with you, as partners in the same covenant.

decisions.choice: at peace
decisions.reason: Readable uses "at peace" for the covenant with the stones, since "covenant" with stones is hard to picture; the second line shows the sense (m1).

source.text: וְֽ֭יָדַעְתָּ כִּי־שָׁל֣וֹם אָהֳלֶ֑ךָ וּֽפָקַדְתָּ֥ נָ֝וְךָ וְלֹ֣א תֶחֱטָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: And you will know that peace [is] your tent, and you will visit your dwelling and not miss.

en.L: And you will know that your tent [is] at peace, \q and you will visit your homestead and not miss [anything].
en.B: You will know that your home is secure; \q you will look over your property and find nothing missing.
en.R: You will know that your home is safe; \q you will check on your land and animals and find that nothing is missing.

decisions.choice: not miss: find nothing lacking
decisions.reason: The verb chata' usually means to sin, but its older sense is to miss a mark (Judges 20:16). When you count what you own, nothing will be missing.

decisions.choice: dwelling: homestead, pasture and flocks
decisions.reason: Naveh is a dwelling or pasture (5:3). Beside "tent" it means the whole homestead with its flocks.

decisions.choice: your tent is at peace: your home is safe
decisions.reason: "Tent" is home, from the days of living in tents. Shalom is wholeness and safety.

decisions.choice: your land and animals
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what a homestead held (m2).

source.text: וְֽ֭יָדַעְתָּ כִּי־רַ֣ב זַרְעֶ֑ךָ וְ֝צֶאֱצָאֶ֗יךָ כְּעֵ֣שֶׂב הָאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: And you will know that many [is] your offspring, and your descendants like the grass of the earth.

en.L: And you will know that your offspring [will be] many, \q and your descendants like the grass of the earth.
en.B: You will know that your offspring will be many, \q your descendants like the grass of the earth.
en.R: You will see that you will have many children, \q and your family will spread like grass across the earth.

decisions.choice: offspring, descendants: children and the family line after them
decisions.reason: Zera' (seed) and tse'etsa'im (what comes out) are a common pair for children and descendants (Isaiah 44:3; 48:19).

decisions.choice: a promise Job cannot hear without pain
decisions.reason: Job's sons and daughters have all died (1:18-19). Eliphaz's picture of the blessed man's many children falls hard on a man who has just buried his own.

decisions.choice: grass: green plants, a picture of abundance
decisions.reason: 'Esev is green growth, which springs up everywhere after rain (Psalm 72:16).

source.text: תָּב֣וֹא בְכֶ֣לַח אֱלֵי־קָ֑בֶר כַּעֲל֖וֹת גָּדִ֣ישׁ בְּעִתּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: You will come in full vigor to [the] grave, as goes up a stack of sheaves in its time.

en.L: You will come in full vigor to [the] grave, \q as a stack of sheaves goes up in its season.
en.B: You will come to your grave in full vigor, \q like sheaves gathered in at harvest time.
en.R: You will live to a ripe old age before you die, \q like grain brought in at the right time.

decisions.choice: full vigor: a ripe old age, strength not yet gone
decisions.reason: Kelach is a rare word, found only here and in 30:2. It seems to mean full strength or ripe maturity: you will die old but not broken.

decisions.choice: a stack of sheaves goes up: grain carried to the threshing floor
decisions.reason: At harvest the cut sheaves were stacked and carried up to the threshing floor. Grain is gathered when it is ripe, neither too early nor too late; so a good life ends at its proper time.

decisions.choice: live to a ripe old age before you die
alternatives: come in full vigor to the grave
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the picture means (m1, m2).

source.text: הִנֵּה־זֹ֭את חֲקַרְנ֥וּהָ כֶּֽן־הִ֑יא שְׁ֝מָעֶ֗נָּה וְאַתָּ֥ה דַֽע־לָֽךְ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: Look, this we have searched it out, so it [is]; hear it, and you, know [it] for yourself.

en.L: Look, this we have searched out; so it [is]. \q Hear it, and know [it] for yourself.
en.B: We have looked into all this, and it is true. \q So hear it and know it for your own good.
en.R: We have studied all this, and it is true. \q So listen, and accept it for your own good.

decisions.choice: we: Eliphaz and the wise whose teaching he passes on
alternatives: Eliphaz and the other two friends
decisions.reason: Eliphaz speaks for the tradition of the wise, what has been searched out and tested over time (8:8-10; 15:9-10, 18).

decisions.choice: for yourself: for your own good
decisions.reason: "For you" after a command means "for your own sake" (Genesis 12:1). Eliphaz ends with confident advice: take this to heart, and it will go well with you.

decisions.choice: no "Look"
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable carry hinneh with the force of the sentence rather than a separate word. Literal keeps "Look".
